blocks.text: Acid rain is an atmospheric mixture of nitric acid and sulphuric acid produced by industrial pollution. Normal rain water has pH up to or above 5.6, due to carbonic acid. If it has a pH lower than 5.6, it potentially becomes the acid rain.

Acid rain is caused due to sulphur oxides (SOₓ) and nitrogen oxides (NOₓ) in the atmosphere. These gases, often from industrial pollution, react with water to form sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄) and nitric acid (HNO₃).

When acid rain falls on soil, it causes a chemical reaction that leaches out essential nutrients like calcium (Ca²⁺), magnesium (Mg²⁺), and potassium (K⁺) from the soil, making them unavailable for plants.

Simultaneously, it can increase the solubility of toxic metals, like aluminium (Al³⁺), which can then be absorbed by the plants' roots and damage them. This reduces the plants' ability to take up nutrients, leading to slower growth and lower crop yields.

blocks.alt: A landscape showing how acid rain forms in a cloud from SOx and NOx emissions and how it affects a lake and the soil.
blocks.caption: Figure 32.3: Effects of acid rain on agriculture (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 32.3).
blocks.long_description: A landscape. Sky: the sun labelled Sunlight with a dotted line to O3; a dark cloud with a box 'Cloud Chemistry: Pollutant Oxidation (SO2, NOx) -> Acid Formation (H2SO4, HNO3) -> Dissolution (Acidic Raindrops)'; rain labelled 'Acid Rain H+, NH4+, NO3-, SO4 2-' and two large drops HNO3 and H2SO4. Right: a factory with smoke labelled 'SOx / NOx Emissions', a house with 'Dry Deposition (SO2 / NOx)', a truck and a car on a road. Ground: 'Natural Ammonia'; a lake with fish, 'Water Acidification (Harmful to Life)'. Left, in a soil section under trees: arrows down, 'Soil Acid Leaching'; H+ arrows to Ca2+ and K+, which are carried away, and to Al3+, 'Aluminum Release (Toxic)'.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In the printed Figure 32.3 the soil arrows run from Ca2+ and K+ to Al3+; as the book's leaching equations say, H+ displaces Ca2+ and K+ (which are leached away) and releases Al3+, as drawn above.

Direct acid rain can damage the leaves, dehydrate them and makes the plant vulnerable to disease and environmental effects. Acid rain can reduce the soyabean and wheat yields by reducing nitrogen fixation and nutrition intake. Acid rain can adversely affect the soil microbial communities, and disrupt the natural nutrient cycles and decomposition of organic matter.

blocks.title: Did You Know?
blocks.text: Why fish die in acidic lakes? Acid rain releases Al³⁺ from soil, which clogs fish gills and reduces oxygen absorption → fish suffocate.
